notes: Deep pass on Second Empire ironwork & balcon filant (1853-1870 canonical haussmannien), sourced entirely from Wikimedia Commons via the API (categorymembers on Category:Place Saint-Michel (Paris), Category:Boulevard de Sébastopol (Paris), Category:Rue Halévy (Paris), plus generator=search on French terms 'balcon filant Paris facade', 'balcon fer forge Paris immeuble XIXe', 'ferronnerie garde-corps Second Empire Paris', and a direct search for avenue de l'Opéra facade views). Deliberately reused the SAME well-attested early-Haussmann streets as the general second-empire family (Place Saint-Michel, Avenue de l'Opéra, Rue Halévy, Rue de Rennes) plus one new one (Boulevard de Sébastopol, pierced 1855-1858, about as early as Second Empire percées get) rather than chasing new neighbourhoods, because period discipline matters more than geographic breadth for this reference family. Every file below is a DIFFERENT Commons image than the ones already used in meta/second-empire.json -- checked every source_url against that file before finalizing; two early picks (a second avenue-de-l'Opéra crop and a boulevard-de-Sébastopol corner shot) turned out to be the exact same Commons files already saved for the general second-empire family and were swapped out for the rue-de-Rennes and boulevard-Sébastopol images now in slots 04 and 05, so nothing here duplicates what that family already has. Two images give both halves of the brief directly: se-ironwork_06 shows a corner building on Boulevard de Sébastopol with '1858' cut into the stone pier itself (a facade-inscribed build date, not a photo-capture date -- the one case in this batch where a year could be recorded with a real source); se-ironwork_02 is a 1916 photograph (Paris Musées, Charles Lansiaux) looking down Avenue de l'Opéra that is the single best 'block unity' image found -- ten-plus party-wall bays of uninterrupted matching balcon filant recorded exactly as the 1855 circulaire intended, with the ironwork itself photographed close to when it was new. Rejected (not saved), by reason: 128 boulevard de Courcelles / rue d'Andigné / rue Raffet / rue Decamps / rue du Général-Delestraint / rue Poussin / rue Davioud balcony detail shots (Category:Balconies in Paris turned these up abundantly) were all dropped as out-of-period -- these are Auteuil (16e) streets built up mostly 1880s-1900s, well past 1870, even though the category lumps them in with genuine haussmannien balconies; avenue Niel and boulevard Haussmann buildings were skipped for the same reason (Niel opened 1868 but built up through the 1880s-90s eclectic idiom; Boulevard Haussmann itself was not completed until 1926, so most of its frontage is Third Republic or later despite the name). '17 quai d'Anjou' (Hôtel de Lauzun) is 17th-century, not Second Empire, and was dropped despite turning up in a balcony search. Several otherwise fine Commons photos were dropped purely on legibility: 11 boulevard de Sébastopol obstructed by bare winter tree branches across the whole frame with a boarded/graffitied ground floor; two more Sébastopol street views (Bvd-de-Sébastopol 02 and 03) where a plane tree and a traffic-sign pole cut across the one legible facade; a boulevard Capucines street view lost to scaffolding and parked vans; a 'Boulevard des Capucines 5' row shot where a modern glass infill building and a later Renaissance-revival neighbour (round-arched windows, looser dressing -- reads as 1880s-90s, not canonical Second Empire) sat next to each other, making the row unusable as a clean example; a Mistinguett commemorative plaque (no facade at all); Place du Châtelet monument/theatre views (Fontaine du Palmier, Théâtre du Châtelet) which show civic monuments, not residential haussmannien elevations; and a Place Saint-Michel garbage-day street photo with the facade reduced to background behind bins and a lamppost. Rue Réaumur was excluded as a search target entirely once its own PDFs turned up ('cérémonie d'inauguration de la Rue Réaumur, le 7 février 1897') confirming the percée is a Third Republic / Belle Époque cut, not Second Empire. Rate-limited heavily by the Commons API during this session (repeated HTTP 429s on both urllib and curl); worked around with a custom User-Agent header and exponential backoff between calls, not by reducing query volume, so the searches above are complete rather than truncated. Dating discipline: 'year' is left blank throughout except se-ironwork_06, where the source is an inscription visible in the photograph itself, not Commons' photo-capture metadata -- the same standard applied to the rest of this corpus. 'klass' is an honest visual read of the fabric shown (all comfortable-to-grand boulevard-front buildings, consistent with the rest of the second-empire family), not a sourced claim.

images.title: 3 place Saint-Michel, balcon, toit
images.author: Coyau
images.shows: Tight upward-angled crop of the corner mansard and the floor just below it: a dense, symmetrical cast-iron balcon-filant balustrade (fine interlocking scrollwork, no whiplash asymmetry) running along the whole visible bay, plus small matching wrought-iron balconettes on the dormer windows in the zinc comble itself. A rule about the standard haussmannien scrollwork pattern, or about ironwork repeating at the attic-storey dormers, is directly answerable to this image.

images.title: 23, avenue de l'Opéra (1916)
images.license: CC0 (Public Domain, Médiathèque de l'architecture et du patrimoine / Paris Musées)
images.author: Charles Joseph Antoine Lansiaux, photographe
images.shows: Long raking street view down the full enfilade: a continuous balcon filant carried across ten-plus separate party-wall bays at a consistent floor line, exactly the block-wide horizontal continuity the 1855 circulaire was written to force. Photograph itself dates to 1916 (irrelevant photo-capture date, not used as a construction date) but the ironwork and stone are photographed close enough to their construction to be undisturbed by later renovation.

images.title: Avenue de l'Opéra, no. 32 (bus view)
images.author: Freepenguin
images.shows: Upper-floor run of continuous balcon filant with dense scrollwork at two separate levels across several adjoining buildings; the ground floor and part of the middle register are cut by open-top-bus seating and a passenger in the foreground, so only the upper facade is usable as evidence.

images.title: Corner building, rue de Rennes, three balcony bands
images.author: Guillaume Baviere
images.shows: Tight B&W corner crop stacking three distinct ironwork bands on the same facade: a full balcon filant at the top floor (with a figure walking on it for scale) in dense symmetrical cast scrollwork, a narrower two-bay balconette band at the floor below in a different, finer foliate pattern, and small individual window balconettes lower still over a mascaron keystone -- good evidence for how the ironwork register changes by floor height on one elevation.

images.title: Boulevard de Sébastopol, street elevation
images.author: Chabe01
images.shows: Clear daylight street view with buildings on both sides showing matching balcon-filant bands at consistent floor heights running the length of the visible block. Boulevard de Sébastopol was pierced 1855-1858, among the very first Second Empire percées, so this street is safely inside the 1853-1870 window.

images.title: Corner building dated 1858, boulevard de Sébastopol
images.author: Sophia0406
images.street: boulevard de Sébastopol, Paris (exact house number not recorded on Commons)
images.shows: Upward corner view with dense, rich cast-iron scrollwork balconies at two consecutive floors, foliage partly overhanging the top-left corner but the ironwork itself fully legible. A construction date, '1858', is cut directly into the stone pier at the corner and clearly visible in the photograph (not a Commons photo-capture date) -- a rare case in this corpus of an on-facade date within the strict 1853-1870 window.

images.title: Fontaine Saint-Michel and adjoining block
images.author: Jorge Láscar
images.shows: Wide panorama of the whole place: on the right, an unbroken run of matching balcon filant and matching 45-degree combles across the full block from the corner around to the side street, visibly the same design repeated building to building -- the clearest 'enforced block unity' composition in this set, even though individual railing patterns read smaller than in the tight crops.

images.title: Immeuble, rue Halévy
images.author: MOSSOT
images.shows: Full, near-frontal facade in even light: two bands of dense symmetrical cast-iron balcon filant (2nd floor and 5th floor under the straight comble), Corinthian-pilaster window surrounds, a mascaron keystone over the ground-floor arch, and pedimented dormers. A clean, unobstructed reference for how the two balcony bands sit relative to the whole elevation.

images.title: Rue Halévy, dormer and balustrade detail
images.author: Vania teofilo
images.shows: Tight upward crop pairing two pedimented dormers on a straight comble with the dense cast-iron balustrade of the balcon filant directly below -- a good answerable image for how the roofline dormer rhythm and the ironwork band relate vertically on the same facade.

images.title: Boulevard de Sébastopol, sidewalk enfilade
images.author: Chabe01
images.shows: Street-level view down a long stretch of sidewalk: a continuous line of cast-iron balconies at matching floor heights recurs down the whole visible block on the right, receding into the distance -- direct visual evidence of the 1855 circulaire's block-wide alignment rule holding over many buildings, not just two.
